Buying well

Common solar purchasing mistakes — and how to avoid them

The decisions that look harmless at quote time and expensive three years later, collected in one checklist.

Published 1 October 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Most solar purchases end well. The ones that end badly tend to fail in predictable ways — not because buyers were careless, but because the industry sells on prices and pictures while the important decisions hide in the details. Here are the mistakes worth engineering out of your process.

The ten that matter

  1. Buying on price per kilowatt alone — the cheapest headline price wins attention for budgets built from weaker products, thinner warranties or rushed installation. Compare specification tables, not just dollars divided by kilowatts.
  2. Accepting a single quote — the market is competitive, and quotes genuinely vary in specification and service. One quote tells you a price; three tell you a market.
  3. Sizing before the roof is assessed — shade, orientation and roof condition are design inputs, not footnotes. A quote produced without them is a guess.
  4. Oversizing to 'profit from exports' — where feed-in rates are low and export limits exist, generation without a use earns little. Size to consumption, or to consumption plus storage.
  5. Skipping battery-readiness when storage is likely — headroom in inverter, switchboard and layout costs little at installation and a great deal to retrofit.
  6. Ignoring the electricity plan — the best system on the wrong tariff underperforms the same system on the right one. Review plans around installation, with Energy Made Easy.
  7. Treating an estimate as a guarantee — savings figures depend on weather, tariffs and behaviour. Demand assumptions and ranges, and distrust single-number promises.
  8. Signing before the paperwork is read — the contract should name models, warranties, incentive treatment, timelines and what happens if conditions change. If that is too much to read on the night, the deadline was invented.
  9. Not verifying accreditation and product lists — check the installer's accreditation and that quoted products appear on the eligible lists for any incentive included in the price. Logos in brochures prove nothing.
  10. Forgetting to ask about after-sales — who answers the phone in year four matters more than a busy month at installation. Ask how service requests are handled and who does the work.

The cheapest quote is rarely the cheapest outcome

A system is a twenty-year appointment with whoever installed it. The difference between the lowest and the middle quote is usually small against the cost of a system that was sized wrong, installed hastily, or orphaned by a company that has moved on to the next suburb.

The pre-signature checklist

  • Consumption-based sizing reasoning, in writing, referencing my actual data.
  • Every model number quoted, with warranty terms for each layer.
  • Generation estimate with its yield and shade assumptions stated.
  • Incentive treatment explained, including what changes the price after signing.
  • Installation scope stated: mounting, switchboard work, monitoring, access and clean-up.
  • After-sales process described: who to contact, expected response, warranty labour position.

Key takeaways

  • Compare specifications and service, not just price per kilowatt.
  • Get multiple quotes; details differ where quality does.
  • Size from consumption and roof reality — never from a template or export dreams.
  • Plan storage headroom if a battery is likely within a few years.
  • Read contracts before signing, and verify accreditation and product eligibility independently.
